## What is Cost Share?
Cost Share Defined
Before diving into the specifics of cost sharing at Morgan State University, it’s essential to address a fundamental question: What exactly is cost share?
Cost share, also known as matching, refers to the portion of a project’s costs that are not covered by the sponsor of the award and are instead borne by MSU or a third party. For example, a private company may offer a piece of equipment to a MSU faculty member for work on a project. Or MSU may partially cover salary costs for project personnel. Assets offered for cost sharing must be allowable and directly allocable to the project (ie. utilized directly to further the goals of the project). Additionally, these resources cannot be derived from previous or active federal funding for cost sharing on federal grants.
Please refer to the following for additional reference to MSU policy and federal law: MSU PI Handbook #5 Uniform Guidance (2CFR200.306)
Complete the content above before moving on.

## Forms of Cost Share
Forms of Cost Share
Cost sharing can be structured in various forms, each tailored to meet specific project or grant requirements, including direct financial contributions, in-kind support like equipment or services, dedicated personnel time, or waived indirect costs. To qualify as cost share, these contributions must be allowable under the funding opportunity announcement (FOA) and directly allocable to the project.
https://cdn.articulate.com/assets/rise/assets/block-defaults/mountains_thumb.jpg
Non-cash contributions such as facilities, equipment, or supplies.
In-Kind Contributions
Actual dollars allocated to the total project budget.
Cash Contributions
Salary and fringe costs for the effort of faculty & technical staff not charged to the sponsor, but contributes directly to the success of the project.
Effort
When such costs are used for advancing the goals of the project but are not reimbursed by the sponsor.
Graduate Student Salaries or Tuition Remission
A reduction of MSU’s negotiated F&A cost recovery. However, only some federal agencies allow for this form of cost sharing.
Unrecovered F&A
Travel expenses directly related to the project but not reimbursed by the sponsor.
Travel Costs
Cost sharing cannot be allocated to more than one project in full. For example, if Morgan State University supports 25% of a faculty member's time as cost share, it is permissible to allocate this time across multiple projects, such as 15% toward one project and 10% toward another. However, applying the full 25% to multiple projects is not allowed. Similarly, for equipment used in cost sharing, usage hours should be tracked and reported separately for each project to ensure accurate allocation.

## Cost Share Classifications
Cost Share Classifications
Let's explore the different ways institutions can contribute to sponsored projects: mandatory, voluntary committed, and voluntary uncommitted cost share. Understanding these distinctions is essential for effective project planning and compliance with funding requirements.
https://cdn.articulate.com/assets/rise/assets/block-defaults/paraglide_thumb.jpg
Mandatory Cost Share
Mandatory cost share is the portion of project or program costs that a grant recipient, such as a university or research institution, is required to contribute as a condition of receiving certain federal or other types of funding. This contribution is stipulated by the funding agency and is usually specified in the funding opportunity announcement or award terms. Mandatory cost share must be honored and properly documented .
Voluntary Committed Cost Share
Voluntary committed cost share is when MSU, in the project proposal and associated budget and budget justification, voluntarily offers to contribute to the project when not required by the sponsor. Once the proposal is approved by the sponsor it becomes a binding obligation. Voluntary committed cost share must be honored and properly documented . Please Note : As a rule, MSU forbids voluntary committed cost share. Voluntary committed cost share generally does not increase a project’s chance of being funded. This type of cost share may also be explicitly prohibited by the FOA. PIs seeking to provide voluntary committed cost share must receive approval from their Chair, Dean, and the Office of Research Administration prior to proposal submission.
Voluntary Uncommitted Cost Share
If cost sharing occurs during the execution of the award, but is not mandated by the FOA or promised in the proposal, it is considered voluntary uncommitted cost share . For instance, if a Principal Investigator (PI) dedicates 35% of their time to a project instead of the 25% originally committed, with the additional 10% covered by the university, this would constitute voluntary uncommitted cost sharing. Since this additional effort is neither required nor formally pledged, it does not represent a binding obligation. There is no mandate for documentation or reporting to the sponsor.

## Cost Share: Pre-Award
Pre Award Planning
Cost sharing at Morgan State University is a significant, long-term commitment that spans the entire lifecycle of a project, from inception through closeout. Meeting these obligations is essential to maintain federal compliance and uphold our institutional commitment to supporting research. Carefully review the following steps to ensure that all necessary actions are taken prior to submitting any proposal with cost-sharing requirements.
Cost Share: Pre-Award Phase
All proposals for sponsored projects must be routed through ORA prior to submission. The Authorized Organizational Representative (AOR) is the only individual authorized to submit applications and accept awards on behalf of MSU.
Step #1: Submit an Internal Routing Form (IRF)
For any proposal submission, a prospective PI must complete an Internal Routing Form (IRF) to provide necessary preliminary information to ORA & the Office of Restricted Funds Accounting (RFA). When a project has mandatory or voluntary committed cost share the PI must check the corresponding box on the IRF.
Step #2: Review Budget with ORA Budget Specialist
During the proposal preparation phase, the ORA Budget Specialist will review the FOA and IRF. If cost share commitments are present, they will ask the PI for elements of cost share and will work with the PI to prepare a budget and budget justification. These documents will be included in the proposal submission.
Step #3: Chair & Dean Approval
If an award has mandatory or voluntary committed cost share, the budget and budget justification must be approved by the PI’s Chair and Dean and provided to the ORA no later than one week prior to the project’s submission deadline.
Step #4: 3rd Party Cost Share
For third party cost share, the PI will be required to provide ORA & RFA with documentation detailing the commitment from the external entity. The PI should provide this documentation no later than one week prior to the proposal submission deadline. Valuation of 3rd party cost share should be in line with market value for similar goods & services.
Complete the content above before moving on.

## Cost Share: Post-Award
Post Award: Documentation and Monitoring
Congratulations on receiving your award! With the Notice of Award (NOA) now in hand, it's essential to establish cost share commitments from day one. To facilitate this, please review the following steps carefully to ensure cost share is accurately recorded in Banner. Proper tracking is critical for accurate sponsor invoicing and maintaining federal fiscal compliance.
Cost Share: Post-Award Phase
Step #1: Initial Award Setup
When the Office of Research Administration receives an NOA with committed cost share the following will happen: A post award briefing will be scheduled with DRED staff, the PI, and their support staff. The briefing will provide resources, allow for questions, and detail the requirements and responsibilities of cost share under the award. ORA Staff will coordinate with Restricted Funds Accounting (RFA) staff to create a Cost Share Activity Code. Use of the activity code is covered later in this lesson.
Step #2: Cost Share Specifics Sent to RFA
The ORA Budget Specialist will send the cost share budget and budget justification to the RFA team.
Step #3: Host a Post Award Briefing
A post award briefing is required for all projects with documented cost share. We will outline the requirements and responsibilities of cost share and determine cost share sources. The project's cost share activity code will be shared with the PI via the RFA team.
Step #4: Complete Cost Share DocuSign Forms
For personnel cost share, a Payroll Cost Share Memo (attached below) must be completed and sent to Crystal Nichols (crystal.nichols@morgan.edu). This form should be completed for any personnel (PI, Co-PI, Program Manager, etc) whose salary will require cost share under the award. It is crucial to verify an employee does not over commit cost share between all projects at MSU. Please review your payroll cost share memo with your RFA account prior to submitting the completed form to Ms. Nichols. For non-personnel cost share, the appropriate Non-Payroll Cost Share Form (below) must be completed on a schedule outlined by the PI's RFA Grant Accountant. This schedule will be based on the invoicing/reporting deadlines of the award. There are two Non-Payroll Cost Share Forms: Non-Payroll Cost Share Memo - Participant Support Costs Non-Payroll Cost Share - Travel, Services, & Commodities
Step #5: Cost Share Activity Code
As a part of the award setup process the MSU RFA team will create a cost share activity code specific to each award. The code typically will reflect the project's fund code with a 'C' at the end. For example, a project with fund code 12345 would have a cost share activity code of 12345C. The code can be used on a variety of expensing instruments to include travel forms, stipend requests, requisitions, and p-card reconciliations. FOAPAL: Banner Grant Codes
When dealing with budgets you will likely come across the acronym FOAPAL. This refers to a string of codes setup by the Restricted Funds Accounting (RFA) team that is unique to a specific budget. FOAPAL stands for:
Fund
A project's fund is a 5-digit code unique to a specific project. Many forms will ask for both a project's index and fund number.
Organization Code
Each group on campus (School of Social Work, GESTAR, etc) has a unique organization code that "houses" a project budget. Typically, budgets under each org code are under the purview of the school's Budget Officer.
Account
Budgets are broken down in Banner into pool levels (noted by 2-digit pool level codes). Each pool level has various 5-digit account codes which impact the corresponding budget. For example, your project's supply pool (09) may have office supply expenses (09021) charged against it.
Program
This helps identify the funding source. For the vast majority of grants on campus the program code will always be 25.
Activity
Many project budgets will not utilize the activity code, but it is used to identify special activity such as cost share on grants. Please review our cost share module for more information on cost share activity codes.
Location
This is typically not used on grants, but may be utilized for fixed assets.

## Budget Transfer Requests
Transferring Funds on Sponsored Projects
What happens if you didn't initially budget for an expense in your approved budget outlined in your Notice of Award (NOA)? There may be times when the needs of your project require funds to move from one budget category to another. This is where the Budget Transfer process comes in.
Complete the content above before moving on.
Restrictions on Budget Transfers
Before submitting a budget transfer request the initiator should consider the factors below.
Sufficient Funds in Pool Level
This may seem obvious, but there must be sufficient funds in the Banner pool level from which you plan to transfer funds. Without enough money the transfer will not be processed.
Allowability
Budget transfers cannot occur if the reason for the transfer is not allowable under the terms of the project award. A common example is equipment. Many projects specifically restrict spending project funds on equipment. If this is the case, a budget transfer will not be approved to move funds to the equipment pool level. Transfer requests should only involve one index per request. Transfers between multiple indexes/projects is not allowable. Budget transfers should not create new budget categories. For example, you should not transfer funds out of supplies to create a new travel budget without prior written sponsor approval.
Change of Project Scope
A budget transfer cannot be processed if doing so would substantially alter the design and scope of the project. If a change in scope would result from the budget transfer it is the PI's responsibility to contact their Program Officer for written authorization to move the funds.
Pool Level & Percentage Change Restrictions
Many sponsors have limitations on how much funding can be moved between the pool levels outlined in the project Notice of Award. For example, NIH-sponsored projects typically limit budget transfers to no more than 25% of the total project budget. Additionally, several Banner pool levels have their own specific restrictions. Some examples include the following: 01&02 (Salaries) : Key Personnel, PIs and CO-PIs, cannot move more than 25% of their proposed salary/effort without approval from the Program Officer. 11 (Equipment) : If your NOA/FOA explicitly restricts equipment purchases then funds cannot be transferred into the 11 Banner pool level. 12 (Participant Support) : Moving funds out of pool level 12 requires written authorization from the project's Program Officer. 15 (Indirect Cost, IDC) : Funds cannot be transferred out of pool level 15 and added to a direct cost pool level such as 09 (Supplies) unless the transfer in/out of pool level 15 is to compensate for funds moving from an IDC-assessed pool level to a non-assessed one. For example, let's say you have a $2,000,000 project with $100,000 in your equipment pool level. Now your project needs have changed and you can use a less-expensive piece of equipment ($50,000) to perform the work without impacting your project scope. To move the excess equipment funds to your travel pool (04) the $50,000 would need to be split between 04 and 15 to account for the increased IDC capture ($32,679 to 04 & $17,321 to 15 based on a 53% IDC rate). IDC is not assessed on activities under pool level 12 (Participant Support), pool level 11 (Equipment), or subawards after IDC is captured on the first 25k of the subaward. Current IDC rates can be found here .

A labor redistribution is the process of moving salary and associated fringe benefit expenses from one funding source to another after payroll has already posted. In sponsored projects, labor redistributions commonly occur in situations such as: Pre-award spending (when authorized), where payroll expenses must temporarily post to a non-sponsored index until the official award/index is established. ## Uniform Guidance: Subpart E
UG: Cost Accounting Standards (CAS) Basics
Subpart E of the Uniform Guidance establishes the federal cost principles used to determine whether costs may be charged to a federal award. For procurement activity, Subpart E helps answer a basic but important question: “Can this purchase appropriately be paid for with grant funds?” These principles require costs to be allowable , allocable to the award, reasonable for the work being performed, and treated consistently with institutional policies and accounting practices. 2 CFR 200.403 , Factors Affecting Allowability of Costs, provides the general standards that must be met before a cost can be charged to a federal award.
Allowability
Allowability asks whether a cost is permitted under the award, federal regulations, sponsor terms, and institutional policy. In procurement, this means the item or service must be necessary for the project and not specifically prohibited, such as entertainment costs, food/catering, or purchases outside the award’s approved purpose.
Allocability
Allocability asks whether the cost benefits the specific project being charged. A purchase should be assigned to a federal award only when that award actually receives the benefit, and if multiple projects benefit, the cost should be distributed in a reasonable and documented way. Please Note: End-of-period spending is highly scrutinized because purchases made near the award end date must clearly benefit the project during the remaining period of performance and cannot simply be used to spend down available funds.
Reasonableness
Reasonableness asks whether a prudent person would consider the purchase appropriate under the circumstances. This includes considering the price, timing, quantity, necessity, and whether the purchase reflects sound business judgment rather than convenience or personal preference.
Consistency
Consistency means costs must be treated the same way across the institution when similar circumstances exist. For example, if Morgan normally treats a certain type of cost as an indirect administrative expense (such as administrative employee salaries), it generally should not be charged directly to a grant unless the award circumstances clearly justify that treatment.

Utilizing Preferred Vendors
Maryland’s procurement framework emphasizes the use of certified small, minority, veteran-owned, and other socioeconomic vendors where appropriate. Under State of Maryland Executive Order 01.01.2024.38 , procurement officers are directed to consider minority vendors when market research identifies two or more certified businesses capable of performing the work or providing the needed goods or services. Procurement's MBE Liaison can assist with identifying a certified firm to meet your procurement needs.
Minority Business Enterprise (MBE)
An MBE is a business certified through Maryland’s MBE Program as being owned and controlled by individuals who meet the program’s eligibility requirements, including minority status, ownership, control, business size, and personal net worth standards. Maryland’s MBE Program is intended to increase opportunities for minority- and women-owned businesses to participate in State contracting, either as prime contractors or subcontractors. Morgan's Goal: 29% of total institutional procurements.
Small Business Reserve (SBR)
The SBR Program is Maryland’s small business set-aside program. When a procurement is designated as SBR, only certified small businesses may compete for that opportunity, helping ensure that small businesses have a fair chance to participate in State procurement. Morgan's Goal: 15% of total institutional procurements.
Veteran-Owned Small Business Enterprise (VSBE)
A VSBE is a certified veteran-owned small business. Maryland’s VSBE Program creates contracting opportunities on State-funded procurements for qualified veteran-owned small businesses, and designated agencies and departments are directed to spend at least 3% of the dollar value of their procurement contracts with certified VSBE firms. Morgan's Goal: 3% of total institutional procurements.
Woman-Owned Businesses
A woman-owned business is generally a business owned, operated, and controlled by one or more women. In Maryland procurement, women-owned businesses may seek certification through applicable programs, including the MBE Program, where certified women-owned firms can count toward MBE participation goals if they meet the program’s requirements. Morgan's Goal: 1% of total institutional procurements.

## MSU: Subawards vs. Subcontracts
What Is a Subaward?
A subaward typically occurs when a primary grantee or institution receives federal funding and then further distributes a portion of those funds to a collaborating entity, often a subrecipient, to perform specific project-related tasks or activities. Subawards are usually utilized when the collaborating institution has a significant role in the project's design, conduct, or outcomes and they are responsible for their own compliance with federal regulations. In contrast, a subcontract is a contractual arrangement where a portion of the federal grant is allocated to a third-party organization or entity to provide specific goods or services related to the research project. Subcontracts are typically used when the collaborating entity is rendering specialized services and operates under the direct oversight of the primary grantee, who maintains control over the research direction and compliance obligations.
A subaward ( 2CFR200.331 ) is issued when a portion of a sponsored project is carried out by another organization that is acting as a subrecipient . In this arrangement, the external entity is responsible for performing a substantive portion of the programmatic work and contributes to overall project objectives. A subcontract (a.k.a. a contractor/vendor agreement ) is used when an external entity is engaged to provide goods and services that support a sponsored project, but does not take part in the programmatic direction or intellectual leadership of the work. The distinction between subawardee and subcontractor should be made prior to proposal submission. Any new subawards created during the performance period of the prime award will require sponsor approval.

A micro-purchase is a low-dollar procurement of supplies or services that falls at or below Morgan State University’s micro-purchase threshold of $5,000 per transaction . ## Equipment: Procurement Best Practices
Equipment Procurement on Sponsored Awards
Equipment purchases require additional planning before the purchase is submitted. For grant purposes, equipment generally means a single item with an acquisition cost of $5,000 or more and a useful life of more than one year . Equipment is excluded from the Modified Total Direct Cost (MTDC) base, meaning indirect costs are not charged on equipment purchases .
Additional Equipment Considerations
Equipment procurements must consider more than just the purchase price. Important factors may include title ownership, related costs, how the asset will be tagged and tracked, and whether the proposed location has the necessary facilities to support its use.

Facility Needs
Before purchasing equipment, the PI and department should confirm that the University has the space, utilities, and long-term support needed to use it successfully. This includes determining whether the equipment will fit in the intended location, whether alternate space is needed, and whether the location can support required utilities such as electrical, water, cooling, ventilation, or other installation needs. If space is needed, contact Morgan's Facilities, Design and Construction Management (FDCM) team early to confirm whether the project’s space needs can be met upon receipt of the Notice of Award.
Total Cost of Ownership
Departments should also consider the full cost of ownership, not just the purchase price. This may include delivery, installation, service agreements, calibration, maintenance, repairs, supplies, software, warranties, and any training needed for MSU faculty or staff to properly operate the equipment.
Equipment Title
Unless the sponsor or award terms state otherwise, title to equipment acquired under a federal award generally vests with the recipient or subrecipient, subject to federal requirements. Federally funded equipment must be used for the project for which it was acquired as long as it is needed. During that time, it should also be made available for use on other federally supported projects or programs, as long as that use does not interfere with the original project. First preference should be given to other projects supported by the same federal agency that funded the equipment. These requirements are outlined in 2 CFR § 200.313(c) .
Asset Tagging
Once equipment is purchased, it must be tagged through MSU Property Control . Tagging supports institutional asset tracking, helps Morgan maintain accurate property records, and allows for appropriate depreciation or amortization of MSU-owned assets. For federally funded equipment, Uniform Guidance also requires property records, physical inventory, safeguards against loss or damage, and adequate maintenance procedures. These requirements are outlined in 2 CFR § 200.313(d) .

## Student Employees: Restrictions and Considerations
Student Contracts: What You Need to Know
Student employee contracts have additional considerations that PIs, and their support staff, must adhere to. Prior to entering a contract for a student, email OHR@morgan.edu to ensure the student is in employee database for EPAF entry.
Hour Restrictions
Student employees are allowed to work up to 20 hours per week during the academic year and 40 hours per week during the summer. This restriction is inclusive of ALL contracts the student may have at MSU. Doctoral students may work up to 40 hours per week year-round.
Can This Student Receive an employment contract?
There are situations where a student cannot be offered an employment contract with MSU. Such situations may include receiving Title III funding, receiving federal stipend support, the student's particular visa status, etc. Moreover, for inclusion in an employment contract, students are required to possess a social security number (SSN). Should a student lack one, the Principal Investigator (PI) is responsible for liaising with the Office of International Student & Faculty Services to facilitate communication with the Social Security Administration. The turnaround time for receiving a SSN is roughly 1-2 weeks so plan ahead. It is vital that PIs speak with prospective student employees before drafting any contracts to determine if there may be other activities that would disallow the employee from working on your project.
Suggested Hourly Rates
The minimum wage in Maryland as of Jan. 1, 2024 is $15 per hour. However, ORA has provided a suggested hourly rate range based on the student's status and experience. While these ranges are generally accepted, the chosen rate may vary by school and project complexity. Undergraduate: $15-20 per hour Graduate: $18-23 per hour Doctoral: $20-25 per hour Further information can be found in PI Handbook #3: Grant-Related Processes .

## Faculty Summer Contracts
Key Information: Division of Academic Affairs
Every spring the Division of Academic Affairs releases a memo which details the specific information necessary for drafting summer contracts. The pertinent information is identified below.
Contract Start/Stop Dates
All summer faculty contracts (grant contracts, summer teaching, etc.) should occur within the start and stop dates listed on the Academic Affairs memo.
Total Working Days
For Summer 2026, there are a total of 52 working days for faculty summer contracts. This excludes Memorial Day, Juneteenth, and Independence Day. This is because the contract term (less than 2.5 months), and the contract start dates, are not sufficient to qualify for claiming these holiday pay days.
Hourly Rate Calculations
For grant-funded contracts ORA requires faculty summer contract hourly rates to match the calculated maximum hourly rate using the formula in the AA memo. A simplified version of the AA memo formula for Summer 2026 is: [(9.5 month salary * .263)/416]
Maximum Summer Salary
The maximum amount a faculty member can earn across ALL summer contracts, including summer teaching, at MSU is limited to 26.3% of their academic contract (9.5 or 12-month).

A contract initiator might find the proposal budget's contractual salaries pool is not inclusive of fringe costs such as unemployment contributions, social security, etc. With this in mind, a PI or their admin may need to factor 9% fringe into their contract. ## Participant Support Costs: Key Points
What Are Participant Support Costs?
Not every payment on a sponsored award is made for work performed or services rendered. In some cases, funds are provided to help an individual join, attend, or benefit from a training or educational experience connected to the award. These are known as participant support costs, and they may include expenses such as stipends, participant travel, registration fees, and other allowable costs that make participation possible. At Morgan State University, the key first step is determining whether the individual is truly a participant or trainee rather than an employee providing services to the project. Once that distinction is clear, the request can be reviewed and processed through the appropriate Morgan procedure with the documentation needed to support compliance.

Participant Cost Submission Tips
Review Notice of Award (NOA) for Restrictions
Are international students eligible to participate in this project? Are there sponsor-specific limits on stipend amounts, such as those that apply to NRSA -funded fellowships? Always review the project’s Notice of Award (NOA) to confirm that participant support costs align with the approved scope of work and are processed in accordance with sponsor requirements, Uniform Guidance, and Morgan State University policy.
Understand Impact in Banner
Participant support costs are typically budgeted to Pool 12 (Participant Support Costs) in Banner. However, certain participant-related expenses may post to other pool levels, such as non-MSU student stipends in Pool 02 (Contractual Salaries) and participant support travel in Pool 04 (Travel) . For awards with substantial participant support activity, it may be helpful to establish a separate project index dedicated to participant support funds. For assistance with this process, please contact the Restricted Funds Accounting (RFA) team at rfa@morgan.edu .
Indirect Costs (IDC) & Budget Transfers
Budget transfers out of the participant support cost pool are generally unallowable without prior written sponsor approval . When submitting any transfer request involving participant support costs, it is critical to provide supporting documentation showing sponsor approval to both the Office of Research Administration ( ORA) Budget Officers and the RFA team . Participant support costs are excluded from the Modified Total Direct Cost (MTDC) base used to calculate indirect costs. Because of this, transferring funds into or out of participant support budgets may affect the project’s indirect cost calculations and should be reviewed carefully. For additional guidance on MTDC calculations, please refer to the Indirect Costs & MTDC lesson of this module.
Stipends are for Support, Not Employment
Stipend support should not be used as a substitute for an employment contract when an employment arrangement is the more appropriate mechanism. For additional guidance on the distinction between stipend support and employment contracts, please refer to the Stipend vs. Contract: Which is Appropriate? lesson of this module.
Types of Participant Support
Stipend Support
Stipend support is a fixed amount paid to a participant to support their involvement in an allowable training, educational, workshop, or research participation activity. It is not compensation for services as an employee.
Participant Travel
Participant travel covers travel costs paid to participants to attend allowable conferences, workshops, trainings, or other sponsored activities.
Tuition Remission
Tuition support covers tuition and associated fees for participants or trainees when the award and sponsor specifically allow that type of participant-related support. This is more common on training-focused awards than on standard research projects, so the award terms should always be checked carefully.
Health Insurance
Health insurance coverage may be provided for trainees on certain training or fellowship-type awards when permitted by the sponsor. This is not a standard participant support category across all federal awards, so it is especially important to confirm sponsor-specific rules.

## Stipend Vs. Contract: Which is Appropriate?
Employee Contract vs. Participant Stipend
Employee
Employment Contract An employment contract is used when the institution pays an employee for work on a sponsored project, such as salary, wages, or summer research contracts. The core idea is compensation for services rendered. Under Uniform Guidance ( 2 CFR 200.430 ), this is employee compensation and is tied to actual work benefiting the award. Hallmarks of a Contract There is a defined service, deliverable, or work expectation. Pay is tied to the work being performed. Documentation often includes scope of work or position description, dates, pay rate, deliverables, approvals, and payment terms. Employee pay usually carries payroll treatment and associated fringe benefit charges.
Participant
Stipend Support A stipend is not pay for services. It is subsistence support given to a participant, fellow, or trainee so they can take part in training or another eligible educational activity. Uniform Guidance includes stipends within participant support costs, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states directly that stipends support living expenses during training and are not employee compensation. The National Science Foundation (NSF) similarly describes participants as people whose primary purpose is learning or receiving training and who receive a stipend rather than salary and fringe benefits. Hallmarks of a Stipend The primary purpose is training or participation, not labor. The amount is often predetermined. It is not based on hours worked. It is not paid in exchange for institutional services like staffing a lab, entering data, coordinating recruitment, or managing project operations. It is only appropriate when the sponsor and the award purpose allow it. At institutes of higher education (IHEs), federal rules say scholarships, fellowships, and student aid are allowable only when the award’s purpose is to provide training to participants and the agency approves the cost.
Ask yourself this simple question: Are we paying this person because we need them to do work for the project, or because we are supporting them while they learn or participate? If the answer is do work , that points to a contract arrangement. If the answer is learn/participate/train , that points to a stipend arrangement.

Indirect Cost Capture & MTDC
Modified Total Direct Costs, or MTDC , is the portion of a project budget that many institutions, including Morgan State, use as the base for calculating indirect costs. In simple terms, MTDC is not the full project budget. Instead, it includes certain direct cost categories while leaving out specific items that are excluded from the indirect cost calculation. At Morgan, this means indirect costs are not assessed on expenses excluded from MTDC, such as participant support costs, equipment, capital expenditures, and the portion of each subaward over $25,000 . Budget Transfers & MTDC
Budget transfers can affect indirect cost needs when funds move between MTDC and non-MTDC cost categories. Costs excluded from the MTDC base, such as participant support, equipment, capital expenditures, and the portion of each subaward over $25,000, do not generate indirect costs. ## Time and Effort Defined
What is Effort Reporting?
What is Time and Effort Reporting?
Time and Effort Reporting is the formal process by which an institution verifies that the salary and wages charged to sponsored projects reasonably reflects the proportion of an individual's total institutional work devoted to those projects. It is not a record of hours worked, but a certification of effort as a percentage of total activities including research, teaching, and administrative duties.
Auditor Assurance
Effort reporting provides sufficient assurance to state and federal auditors that appropriate internal control measures actively track allocability for each sponsored project. Auditors are looking for: (1) documentation support (2) reasonableness (3) timeliness and (4) internal controls.
Federally Mandated
Effort reporting is a federally mandated requirement outlined in Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Under which, we in the research administration reference Uniform Guidance (2CFR200) as our playbook for research compliance. 2CFR200.430 specifically details personnel compensation and effort on sponsored projects.

Effort certification confirms that salary charged to a sponsored project reasonably reflects the work performed. ## Significance of Effort Reporting
Effort Certification: Institutional Impact
Effort reporting is more than an administrative requirement. It is a formal certification that salary charged to a sponsored project reasonably reflects the work performed. When effort is not certified accurately or in a timely manner, the consequences can extend beyond one project and place the university's federal funding, audit standing, reputation, and future grant eligibility at risk.

Key Institutional Risks
Disallowed Costs and Repayment
If salary charges cannot be supported by accurate effort certification, the sponsor may determine that the costs are unallowable. The university may be required to repay those costs, including associated fringe benefits and indirect costs.
Increased Federal Scrutiny
Poor effort reporting can lead to additional sponsor review, expanded audits, corrective action plans, and stricter award conditions. Under 2CFR200.339 , federal agencies may withhold payments, disallow costs, suspend or terminate awards, initiate suspension/debarment proceedings, withhold future federal funds, or pursue other legal remedies.
Loss of Current or Future Funding
Federal agencies may suspend or terminate awards and may withhold new or continuation funding when noncompliance is serious or unresolved.
Suspension or Debarment Risk
In serious cases, federal agencies may initiate suspension or debarment proceedings. This can affect an institution's ability to receive federal grants, contracts, or other federal funding.
The False Claims Act
The False Claims Act, sometimes called The Lincoln Law, is a federal civil fraud law used to recover funds when an entity knowingly submits, or causes the submission of, false or fraudulent claims for payment to the federal government. This can include knowingly charging salary to an award when certified effort does not support the charge. The False Claims Act can result in significant financial penalties, including damages and penalties per false claim. The Justice Department recovered over $6.8 billion in False Claims Act cases in 2019.

Institutional Base Salary: Contract Restrictions
Faculty Contracts & IBS
For 9.5-month faculty, IBS consists of: (1) their 9.5-month academic year salary , and (2) up to 2.5 months of summer salary . This means faculty may receive additional compensation on sponsored projects during the summer months, but only within defined limits. Staff Contracts & IBS
For 12-month faculty and staff, IBS is defined as their full 12-month institutional salary , which already represents 100% effort . Key Restrictions Individuals cannot exceed 100% IBS Secondary contracts for additional pay on sponsored projects are not allowable Instead of additional compensation, release time or effort reallocation is possible. Administrative/clerical salaries cannot be charged directly when: (1) the work is routine (e.g., general admin support), (2) the role supports multiple projects or departments broadly, or (3) it is not specifically justified and approved in writing. For example, managing a complex training program with many participants. The role must be explicitly included in the proposal budget and justified to the sponsor. ## Booking a Flight or Train Ticket
Flight & Train Costs
Travel Form (TL) Required
A Travel Authorization (TL) Form is required to book a flight or train ticket. Please submit with enough lead time to allow for form approval and processing. The steps to submit a TL form are outlined later in this module.
Using Globetrotter
Globetrotter (1-888-337-2462) is the State of Maryland travel agency. We must utilize Globetrotter to book any flight or train ticket needed on University travel. Call them to get a quote for your flight so you have a reasonable estimate of the expected flight cost. You may also look up your preferred flight online to estimate your flight costs.
Traveler Info
When calling Globetrotter to book a flight be sure you have the traveler's full legal name, birthdate, and contact phone number. Additionally, collect frequent flier or reward account numbers from the traveler so they are applied to the fare.
Fly America Act
The Fly America Act (49 USC 40118) requires federally funded travelers to use US flag air carriers whenever possible, even when cheaper options are available. Make sure you verify this act is adhered to by Globetrotter when making arrangements.
Baggage Fees
Check with your chosen airline to determine what baggage fees may apply for your flight. Any such charges should be included under "Portage" on the MSU Travel Form.

## Additional Travel Rules
Supplemental Travel Policies
Hotel & Other Lodging
Travel destination must be more than 40 miles from MSU campus for lodging expenses to be allowable. AirBNB is prohibited. Tax charges & lodging fees are allowed for hotel/lodging expenses. If the traveler does not have a University Purchasing Card at check-in, an admin with a p-card tied to your grant must submit a Credit Card Authorization Form prior to your stay.
